806.title: Ali's words
806.hook: sermons and sayings attributed to Ali, gathered in Nahj al-Balagha, are especially treasured by Shia Muslims
806.howItsDone: Shia Muslims read Nahj al-Balagha for guidance, study it in seminaries and quote it in sermons; Sunni readers also study it, especially for its Arabic style.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ali ibn Abi Talib, Haydar the lion, and Abu Turab asleep in the dust. Your line was the lion and the scholar.

A governor is about to leave for his new province, and a letter is put in his hands. It tells him how to treat the people he'll rule, and somewhere in it is a line worth stopping on: people are of two kinds. Either your brother in faith, or your equal in creation. The letter is attributed to Ali, written to Malik al-Ashtar as he went to govern Egypt. It's one of many pieces gathered in a single book. Today: Ali's words.
screen: `A LETTER TO A GOVERNOR.` → `TWO KINDS OF PEOPLE.` → `A BROTHER, OR AN EQUAL.`

segments.voice: The book is called Nahj al-Balagha, the path of eloquence. Its compiler gathered sermons, letters and short sayings attributed to Ali, arranged in those three parts. Shia Muslims treasure it especially, reading it alongside the Qur'an and the hadith as words from their first Imam. Sunni readers have also prized it, often for the beauty of its Arabic, and some scholars question whether every piece in it goes back to Ali himself. So this path says attributed, and means it. Now, the words. Either your brother in faith, or your equal in creation. It leaves nobody out. If someone shares your religion, they're your brother or sister. If they don't, they still came from the same Maker as you, and they're owed the same justice. For a ruler about to hold power over many kinds of people, that's a job description. A short saying is about worth: the value of each person lies in what they do well. The saying doesn't name family or wealth. Only what they do well. And a long letter of advice to his son al-Hasan includes this, in paraphrase: make yourself the measure between you and others. Want for them what you want for yourself, and dislike for them what you dislike for yourself. Don't be anyone's slave when God made you free. All three are short enough to carry. This is where the first circle closes: Abu Bakr, Umar, Uthman and Ali, four men around the Prophet, each remembered in his own way.

807.title: Khadijah, first believer
807.hook: the angel brings a message for one woman alone: greetings of peace from her Lord (Bukhari)
807.howItsDone: Muslims honor Khadijah among the mothers of the believers, and her words on the night of the first revelation, from Sahih al-Bukhari, are often retold when the beginning of the revelation is taught.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ali's words, a brother in faith, or an equal in creation. Your line was words from Ali. Today a new stretch begins: the mothers of the believers.

Peace, from her Lord. In a report preserved by Bukhari, the angel Jibril says to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him: here is Khadijah, coming to you with a vessel of food. When she reaches you, give her greetings of peace from her Lord, and from me. A message from heaven, addressed to one person by name, about to arrive with her hands full. The Qur'an calls the Prophet's wives mothers of the believers. Today, the first of them: Khadijah.
screen: `SHE COMES WITH A VESSEL OF FOOD.` → `JIBRIL NAMES HER.` → `PEACE FROM HER LORD.`

segments.voice: First, the title of this stretch. Surah thirty-three, verse six, in Pickthall: "The Prophet is closer to the believers than their selves, and his wives are (as) their mothers." So for the next days we meet them one at a time. Why is Khadijah greeted like this? Go back to the night everything began. Bukhari's account of the first revelation has the Prophet coming home from the cave of Hira shaking: cover me, cover me. He tells Khadijah he fears for himself. She answers not with a theory but with a list of what she has watched him do. Never, she says. By Allah, Allah will never disgrace you. You keep the ties of family. You carry the burden of the weak. You give to those who have nothing. You honor your guest. You stand by people when trouble comes. Then she takes him to her cousin Waraqah, who knew the earlier scriptures, to hear what it might mean. Tradition remembers her as the first to believe him: by trusting the character she knew, when he himself was afraid. Aisha says in Bukhari that she never felt jealous of any woman the way she did of Khadijah, though she never saw her, because the Prophet spoke of her so often, and would send gifts to her friends. Then the greeting itself. In the same report, Jibril adds glad news: a house in Paradise for her, made of hollow pearl, with no noise in it and no weariness. The one who steadied him in a frightening night is promised a place of quiet.

808.title: Sawdah, who made him smile
808.hook: a widow who joins his household after Khadijah, remembered for her humor and her open hand
808.carry: the one who made him smile
808.howItsDone: Muslims count Sawdah bint Zam'ah among the mothers of the believers; the reports of her giving her day to Aisha and her early leaving at Muzdalifah come from Sahih al-Bukhari, and the stories of her humor from the early biographers.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Khadijah, the one who steadied him, and the peace sent to her from her Lord. Your line was greeted by her lord.

A long night prayer. Bowing, and bowing, and still bowing. Afterward, a woman of his household who prayed behind him comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and says: I prayed behind you last night, and you bowed so long I held my nose, in case it started to bleed. And he laughs. That small joke is how Ibn Sa'd's book of early lives remembers her. She was a widow, the biographers say, who came into his household after Khadijah died, a house that had just lost its center. Today: Sawdah.
screen: `A VERY LONG BOW.` → `I HELD MY NOSE.` → `AND HE LAUGHED.`

segments.voice: Sawdah doesn't arrive in the story with a battle or a revelation attached to her name. She arrives in the ordinary rooms of a grieving home, and she brings lightness into them. The reports about her are small, and that is the point of them. First, her humor. The joke about the long bow is a report in Ibn Sa'd, not in the two Sahih collections, so hold it as a story the early biographers kept. It shows a person who could make the Prophet laugh about a long night of prayer, without making fun of the prayer. The laugh was at herself. Second, her generosity, and this one is in Bukhari. When she grew older, Sawdah gave her turn, her day with the Prophet, to Aisha. Something she could have held on to, she handed to someone else, freely. Third, how the other wives saw her. In Sahih Muslim, Aisha says she never saw a woman she would rather be in the skin of than Sawdah, and adds, honestly, that Sawdah had a certain sharpness. A real person, then: quick, funny, a little fierce, and generous. And one more scene from Bukhari. At the pilgrimage, Bukhari describes her as heavy and slow-moving, and she asked permission to leave Muzdalifah early, before the crowds. He gave it. Aisha later wished she had asked too. Put these together and Sawdah is remembered less for one great act than for the weather she made in a house: a laugh after a long night, a day handed over, an early start before the crowds.

809.title: Aisha the scholar
809.hook: the companions brought her their hard questions, and she corrected them from the Qur'an and from what she had seen
809.howItsDone: Muslims learning hadith meet Aisha as a narrator again and again, and her corrections of other companions are studied as part of how the early community checked what it heard.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Sawdah, her joke about the long bow, and the day she gave to Aisha. Your line was the one who made him smile.

A report is being passed along. It comes from a respected companion, and it says the dead are punished because their families weep for them. Then it reaches Aisha, the Prophet's wife, and she does not simply nod. In the account in Bukhari, she says, in effect: may Allah have mercy on him, but that is not what the Messenger said. And she reaches for the Qur'an to answer it. Today: Aisha the scholar.
screen: `A HARSH REPORT GOES AROUND.` → `IT REACHES AISHA.` → `THAT IS NOT WHAT HE SAID.`

segments.voice: Aisha lived beside the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in the small rooms next to the mosque. After his death, people came to her door with questions, and the hadith collections keep her answers. Here is how she answered the report about weeping. She said the Prophet had spoken about a particular person, not about all the grieving. And she pointed to a principle the Qur'an states more than once: no soul carries the burden of another soul. A family's tears cannot be counted against the one they mourn. That is the scholar's move: test what you hear against the text, and against what you witnessed. She did it again when some said a woman passing in front of a man at prayer cuts off his prayer, as a donkey or a dog would. In Bukhari, she answers sharply: you have made us equal to donkeys and dogs. I used to lie stretched out in front of him while he prayed. She was an eyewitness, and she used it. And the companions noticed. Tirmidhi preserves the words of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari: whenever a hadith puzzled them, they asked Aisha, and found knowledge with her. Her nephew Urwa learned from her and taught others in turn. A later scholar, al-Zarkashi, gathered her corrections of other companions into a book of their own. So when Muslims speak of the mothers of the believers as teachers, this is a large part of what they mean: a woman at home, with a door that kept opening, and a habit of checking the words.

segments.voice: Think of something about faith, or about this path, that you've heard repeated and never checked: a saying, a rule, a story. If you pray, ask for knowledge that helps.

810.title: Hafsah, keeper of pages
810.hook: Umar's daughter, in whose house the gathered sheets of the Qur'an were kept (Bukhari)
810.howItsDone: Muslims who study how the Qur'an was gathered learn the reports in Sahih al-Bukhari of Zayd ibn Thabit's collection under Abu Bakr and Uthman's copying from the sheets kept by Hafsah.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Aisha, who checked what she heard against the text and her own eyes. Your line was she taught the teachers.

A messenger knocks at a woman's door with a request from the caliph Uthman. Please send us the sheets, so we can copy them. We will return them to you. What she has in her house is not jewelry and not a treasury. It is a set of written pages, gathered by careful hands, that she has been trusted to keep. The whole community is about to depend on them. Today: Hafsah.
screen: `A KNOCK FROM THE CALIPH.` → `SEND US THE SHEETS.` → `WE WILL RETURN THEM.`

segments.voice: Hafsah was the daughter of Umar ibn al-Khattab and a wife of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him. Her place in this story comes from two reports in Sahih al-Bukhari, told one after the other. The first is a gathering. After a battle in which many who knew the Qur'an by heart were killed, Umar urged Abu Bakr to collect the Qur'an in writing. Abu Bakr hesitated: how could he do something the Prophet had not done? In the end he agreed, and gave the task to Zayd ibn Thabit. Zayd says it would have been easier to move a mountain. He searched for the verses, gathering them from what was written and from the memories of men. The sheets, Bukhari says, stayed with Abu Bakr until he died, then with Umar for the rest of his life, and then with Hafsah, daughter of Umar. The second report is the knock at her door. In Uthman's time, people in distant lands were reciting differently and arguing over it. Uthman sent to Hafsah, asking for the sheets so they could be copied, with a promise to return them. She sent them. Copies were made and sent out to the regions, and the sheets went back to Hafsah. Look at what kind of honor this is. Hafsah did not write the pages or gather them. She kept them. When the community needed a trusted standard, it knew exactly whose house to ask, and the pages came back to the place they had been safe. Keeping is quiet work, and it is real work.

811.title: Umm Salamah
811.hook: her counsel breaks a silence at Hudaybiyyah, and her question is answered by a verse of the Qur'an
811.howItsDone: Muslims recite surah 33:35 as a verse naming believing men and women side by side, and retell Umm Salamah's advice at Hudaybiyyah from Sahih al-Bukhari as an example of wise counsel.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Hafsah, and the sheets that went out for copying and came back to her house. Your line was she kept the pages.

Nobody moves. The Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, has just agreed a treaty at Hudaybiyyah, outside Mecca, and the terms feel to his companions like a defeat. He tells them: get up, sacrifice your animals, and shave your heads. Bukhari says not one of them rose. He says it again. And again. Silence. So he goes into his tent, to his wife, and tells her what has happened. Today: Umm Salamah.
screen: `A TREATY THAT FEELS LIKE DEFEAT.` → `NOT ONE OF THEM ROSE.` → `HE GOES IN TO HIS WIFE.`

segments.voice: Her advice, in Bukhari, is short and wise. Go out, she says, and don't say a word to anyone. Sacrifice your own animal, and call your barber to shave your head. He does exactly that. And when the companions see it, they get up, sacrifice, and start shaving one another, crowding so hard in their distress that it looked as if they might hurt each other. Umm Salamah understood something about grief and pride: people who won't be argued into moving can sometimes be shown. That's the first thing she's remembered for: counsel in a hard hour. The second is a question. In a report in the Musnad of Ahmad, Umm Salamah asks the Prophet: why are we, the women, not mentioned in the Qur'an the way the men are? She doesn't say it in a corner; she asks him directly. And then, the report says, she heard him reciting from the pulpit a new verse, surah thirty-three, verse thirty-five. In Pickthall it begins: "Lo! men who surrender unto Allah, and women who surrender". It goes on like that, pair after pair: men who believe and women who believe, men who are truthful and women who are truthful, men who give charity and women who give charity, men who fast and women who fast, all the way to forgiveness and a vast reward. The verse speaks to women and men alike. The report adds a story behind it: someone asked. Her question didn't ask for less from women. It asked to be named.
screen: `GO OUT AND SAY NOTHING.` · `SACRIFICE, AND THEY ALL FOLLOW.` · `WHY ARE WE NOT MENTIONED?` · `MEN WHO SURRENDER, AND WOMEN WHO SURRENDER.` · then, large: `SHE ASKED, AND IT CAME.`

segments.voice: Think of a room you're part of, a family, a team, a congregation, a class, and whether there's someone, or something, nobody ever mentions there. Let the question form, as plainly as Umm Salamah's, and just hold the words for now. If you pray, bring that question to Allah, as she brought hers to the Prophet.
Umm Salamah. The mother of the believers whose counsel moved the silent camp at Hudaybiyyah, and whose question is linked to the verse that names women and men side by side. Today's word.
Your line: she asked, and it came. One plain question, and a verse that names women and men side by side. Day eight hundred eleven.

812.title: Zaynab bint Jahsh
812.hook: the wives measure their hands to solve a riddle, and the answer turns out to be charity (Muslim)
812.howItsDone: Muslims retell the hadith of 'the longest hand' from Sahih Muslim when speaking of charity, and honor Zaynab bint Jahsh among the mothers of the believers for giving from the work of her hands.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Umm Salamah, who advised silence at Hudaybiyyah and asked to be named. Your line was she asked, and it came.

Who will be first? In Sahih Muslim, Aisha tells it. The Prophet had said to his wives that the one of them with the longest hand would be the quickest to join him after his death. So they measured their hands, side by side, to see whose was longest. It sounds like a party game: wives holding out their arms, comparing fingertips. And they missed what he meant. Today: Zaynab bint Jahsh.
screen: `WHO WILL FOLLOW HIM FIRST?` → `THE LONGEST HAND.` → `THEY MEASURED.`

segments.voice: The wives took the words of the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, literally, and looked for the longest arm. But Aisha says the longest hand among them was Zaynab bint Jahsh's, because she used to work with her hands and give in charity. Tradition says she was the first of the wives to follow him in death. The riddle was never about length. It was about reach: how far a person's hands went toward others. In Arabic the phrase is atwalukunna yadan, the longest of you in hand. The report itself shows what a long hand meant: a giving one. Notice where her giving came from. Zaynab didn't only hand over what she had. She made things, the report says, and gave from the work of her own hands. Charity that has your fingerprints on it. Notice also who tells us this. Aisha and Zaynab were rivals in the household; the reports don't hide it. Yet it is Aisha who preserves Zaynab's best memory. In another report in Muslim, Aisha describes her as unmatched in her religion, in her fear of Allah, in truthfulness, in keeping ties of family, and in giving charity. And in the account of the slander against Aisha, Bukhari has Zaynab asked what she knew, and answering that she knew nothing but good of her. The two women spoke well of each other when it counted. The longest hands, it turns out, also reached across a rivalry.
screen: `THEY MEASURED THEIR HANDS.` · `SHE WORKED, AND SHE GAVE.` · `A LONG HAND IS A GENEROUS ONE.` · `RIVALS WHO SPOKE WELL OF EACH OTHER.` · then, large: `THE LONGEST HANDS.`

segments.voice: Rest your hands open on your knees, and look at them. Think of one thing they could make or do for someone else, bake something, mend something, write a note by hand, carry someone's bags, something with your fingerprints on it, and picture your hands doing it. If you pray, ask that your hands reach a little further.
Atwalukunna yadan, 'the longest of you in hand,' the riddle about reach, not length, that named Zaynab bint Jahsh, who gave from her own hands' work. Today's word.
Your line: the longest hands. Reach, not length, and across a rivalry too. That's day eight hundred twelve.
